claims.text: The classified evaluation is Report No. DODIG-2023-109, 'Evaluation of the DoD's Actions Regarding Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena,' dated August 15, 2023. A 16-page unclassified summary was published January 24-25, 2024; it carries the note: 'A classified version of the Evaluation of the DoD's Actions Regarding Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena formed the basis of the unclassified summary.'

claims.source: https://media.defense.gov/2024/Jan/25/2003381266/-1/-1/1/UNCLASSIFIED%20SUMMARY_UNIDENTIFIED%20ANOMALOUS%20PHENOMENA%20SECURE.PDF — DEMOTED from Tier 1 (sourced to an interested party (AARO/DoD) asserting an external fact; primary record of the statement, not of the fact); needs primary replacement
claims.text: Core finding, 'The DoD Does Not Have a Comprehensive, Coordinated Approach to Address UAP': 'the DoD has not used a coordinated approach to detect, report, collect, analyze, and identify UAP; DoD Components have largely excluded geographic combatant commands... in developing UAP policies and procedures; and DoD Components developed varying processes to collect, analyze, and identify UAP incidents.'

Consequence finding: 'We determined that the DoD has no overarching UAP policy and, as a result, it lacks assurance that national security and flight safety threats to the United States from UAP have been identified and mitigated.'

On the absence of a response plan: 'The DoD has not issued a comprehensive UAP response plan that identifies roles, responsibilities, requirements, and coordination procedures... As a result, the DoD response to UAP incidents is uncoordinated and concentrated within each Military Department. Officials from the Military Services and MDCOs stated that they have been waiting for the DoD to issue comprehensive UAP guidance before developing their own guidance.'

Recommendation 1: 'We recommend that the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security, in coordination with the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office Director, issue a Department of Defense policy to integrate unidentified anomalous phenomena roles, responsibilities, requirements, and coordination procedures into existing intelligence, counterintelligence, and force protection policies and procedures. The policy should include methods to address unidentified anomalous phenomena incidents and should align with policies and procedures for the protection of United States persons' civil liberties.' USD(I&S) and the AARO Director agreed; the recommendation was left 'resolved but open'.

claims.source: https://media.defense.gov/2024/Jan/25/2003381266/-1/-1/1/UNCLASSIFIED%20SUMMARY_UNIDENTIFIED%20ANOMALOUS%20PHENOMENA%20SECURE.PDF — DEMOTED from Tier 1 (sourced to an interested party (AARO/DoD) asserting an external fact; primary record of the statement, not of the fact); needs primary replacement
claims.text: Historical framing in the summary: 'Over the past decades, the DoD has initiated infrequent and inconclusive efforts to identify and understand the origin, capabilities, and intent of unidentified aerial phenomena (UAP)... the DoD has relied heavily on the Services and Components to detect, report, collect, analyze, and identify UAP since the 1940s.' It counts 243 sightings investigated under PROJECT SIGN (1947-1949) and 'over 12,000 reported sightings' under PROJECT BLUE BOOK (1952-1969).

The IG's finding that DoD had no overarching UAP policy and 'lacks assurance' that threats were identified or mitigated is a primary-record statement of institutional incapacity, not of concealment; it is nonetheless the strongest official acknowledgment on the record that DoD's UAP handling was uncoordinated across the very period in which AARO was assuring Congress the historical record was fully reviewed. Reasoning: the IG evaluation (Aug 2023) and HRR Vol I (Feb 2024) overlap in period and subject but reach differently scoped conclusions.

desc: The Inspector General's evaluation of how the Department handles UAP, completed 15 August 2023 and released in unclassified summary on 25 January 2024. The full report is classified; the public has the summary only. Its findings are structural and damning in an undramatic way: the Department has no overarching UAP policy; different DoD components each developed their own separate processes for collecting, analysing and identifying UAP incidents; and as a result the Department cannot ensure that national security and flight safety threats from UAP have been identified and addressed. It made eleven recommendations to the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security, the service secretaries and the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs, including development of a department-wide policy to integrate UAP roles, responsibilities, requirements and coordination procedures into existing intelligence, counterintelligence and force protection policies. For this board the finding that matters is the fragmentation one. An office that formally reviews only what it can reach, inside a department the IG says has no unified UAP process and component-level stovepipes, cannot produce a negative finding of departmental scope - and every AARO negative finding since has been phrased as 'AARO has discovered no evidence', which is a statement about AARO's reach, not the Department's contents. The classification of the full report means the IG's own account of where the stovepipes are remains unavailable, including through PURSUE.
